name: Deferral of additional suites until pilot data quality thresholds are demonstrated
consequences: Delaying expansion preserves data integrity and safety during the pilot and avoids oversaturation, but it slows enrollment momentum. The gap is the absence of explicit, measurable ramp thresholds that account for night-to-night variability and site performance when deciding the next capacity step.
options: Proceed with 12-suite expansion only after the pilot demonstrates high data quality, acceptable false-alarm rates, and verified annotation throughput across a representative sample of nights.
Maintain an 8-suite launch and optimize scheduling, staffing, and night coverage to maximize usable data without expanding capacity.
Test a modular annex to add two temporary suites under flexible lease terms while collecting performance metrics and user feedback to inform a future expansion decision.
review: Primary trade-off: delaying expansion preserves quality but slows throughput; the gap is the absence of explicit ramp thresholds and a plan that accommodates night-to-night variability.

name: Sensing architecture optimization path
consequences: Shifting modalities changes signal quality, data storage, and staffing needs; enhancing data richness can improve event characterization but raises maintenance overhead. The gap is a clear, quantitative mapping from modality changes to expected improvements in detection sensitivity and annotation throughput.
options: Calibrate and stabilize baseline dry-electrode EEG, mattress sensors, and infrared cameras to establish a robust, low-burden data baseline before adding higher-cost modalities.
Introduce richer PSG components only on enhanced nights after automated quality checks demonstrate consistent data capture from baseline modalities.
Phase in privacy-preserving data streams by adding environmental sensors with strict access controls and on-demand de-identified exports.
review: Primary trade-off: richer sensing improves data but increases cost and burden; the gap is missing explicit thresholds tying modality expansion to measurable gains.

name: Tiered recruitment funnel with structured pre-screening
consequences: Balancing inclusivity with data consistency reduces screen-failures but may slow participant intake and prolong the study timeline. The gap is lack of a real-time monitoring dashboard to adjust inclusion criteria and incentives based on observed yield.
options: Implement a tiered pre-screening funnel with structured clinical interviews and collateral history to minimize screen-failures and align enrollment with event-yield targets.
Offer transportation stipends and flexible scheduling to boost participation while maintaining inclusion criteria that support consistent data collection.
Engage matched controls via hospital networks to streamline comparisons without broadening the enrollment base.
review: Primary trade-off: stricter screening improves data consistency but slows enrollment; the gap is lacking a live yield-tracking mechanism to tune criteria responsively.

name: Privacy-preserving data-sharing governance with staged data releases
consequences: Expanding data sharing increases visibility and collaboration but heightens privacy risk; the gap is lacking concrete governance details to enforce consent, de-identification, and access controls during multi-party use.
options: Publish de-identified physiological and sensor datasets under strict data-use agreements to balance openness with participant privacy.
Implement opt-in video masking for bedroom footage with strict governance to preserve privacy while enabling supplementary behavioral analyses.
Phase data releases with controlled access portals, granting subsets to trusted collaborators before wider dissemination.
review: Primary trade-off: openness vs. privacy; the gap is a concrete governance framework detailing consent processes, de-identification standards, and access controls.

name: Industry partnership terms that protect publication rights
consequences: Industry funding can accelerate progress but may influence dissemination; the gap is ensuring terms and a governance mechanism that prevents delayed publications or biased reporting while preserving academic autonomy.
options: Negotiate industry collaborations with explicit publication rights and data access terms that preserve core academic outputs.
Pursue additional non-dilutive public funding and European research consortia to extend the pilot and widen data resources.
Form a multi-site grant proposal with other sleep centers to share recruitment and cross-site validation while maintaining independent publication rights.
review: Primary trade-off: industry involvement risks publication control; the gap is lacking clear, enforceable terms that safeguard timely, unbiased reporting.

name: Semi-automated event triage with human-in-the-loop
consequences: Automation reduces manual review load but can miss subtle events or introduce biases if not properly calibrated. The gap is a robust fallback for disagreements between algorithm flags and human scorers.
options: Prototype a semi-automated event triage pipeline that flags high-fidelity events for rapid double-scored review by two independent raters.
Strengthen scorer reliability by instituting blinded scoring rounds and standardized calibration sessions before official scoring.
Schedule regular retrospective audits of algorithm-flagged events to identify biases and adjust weighting thresholds accordingly.
review: Primary trade-off: automation vs. detection gaps; the gap is a defined mechanism for resolving disagreements and correcting biases over time.

name: Regional collaboration for participant funnel optimization
consequences: Expands enrollment velocity and diversifies the participant pool, accelerating progress toward Aim 1. However, it introduces cross-site governance and potential variability in screening quality unless SOPs and IRB approvals are harmonized.
options: Formalize referral agreements with regional sleep clinics to funnel eligible participants into Bonn's residential unit while aligning screening criteria and consent processes.
Launch targeted outreach to neighboring university hospitals and neurology clinics to broaden referrals and reduce pre-screening backlogs.
Deploy mobile pre-screening clinics at community centers to identify eligible participants efficiently while maintaining ethical consent and eligibility verification.
review: Regional recruitment reduces enrollment time but increases multi-site coordination overhead; the three options leave unaddressed how to ensure uniform data quality controls and IRB alignment across partners.

name: Tiered sensing calibration and data quality management
consequences: A more aggressive sensing approach improves data resolution and reduces manual review burden, but it raises equipment costs, training needs, and daily maintenance demands. This trade-off constrains staffing flexibility and requires ongoing vendor support.
options: Fully implement nightly dry-electrode EEG headbands with automated artifact rejection to standardize data capture and reduce technician workload.
Maintain the current tiered approach but add randomized mid-study nights with enhanced PSG to validate data fidelity and artifact handling.
Limit enhanced nights to participants with flagged events to conserve resources while risking missed captures of infrequent episodes.
review: Automated artifact rejection reduces manual scoring but relies on robust calibration; gaps include potential misclassification during artifact-rich periods and the need for ongoing validation.

name: Governance of data sharing and privacy versus collaboration
consequences: Expands collaborative opportunities by improving data accessibility while maintaining privacy safeguards; however, broader sharing increases compliance workload and potential delays in data release.
options: Finalize de-identification standards and access controls to enable broader secondary analyses while preserving video data privacy.
Negotiate tiered data-use agreements with external researchers to balance openness with institutional IP protections and governance frameworks.
Implement a controlled-access data portal with audit trails and reviewer workflows to vet research requests before data release.
review: Broad data sharing raises privacy management overhead and potential slowdowns; the three options do not specify how to enforce timely reviews or monitor breaches.

name: Safety-first staffing and operations protocol
consequences: Strengthened coverage and rapid response during nights improve participant safety and data integrity, but may increase training costs and complicate scheduling. This requires ongoing supervision to maintain morale and competency as the program scales.
options: Institute an on-call, cross-trained technician pool to cover peak nights and maintain safety without expanding full-time headcount.
Adopt a staggered shift schedule with backup rosters to ensure continuous coverage during high-risk periods.
Deploy automated alarm escalation systems paired with periodic drills to reduce response times while maintaining minimal on-site presence.
review: On-call staffing enhances safety but can incur idle-time costs and scheduling complexity; gaps include how to sustain morale and training efficiency as capacity scales.

name: Funding structure and publication rights strategy
consequences: This lever clarifies incentives and risk sharing; diversification reduces dependency on any single partner but may slow procurement cycles and complicate governance.
options: Negotiate industry partnership terms that preserve publication rights while offering milestone-based funding and explicit pre-publication review windows.
Pursue diversified funding from foundations and government grants to reduce reliance on industry partnerships and streamline administration.
Establish staged IP and data-access agreements that allow external researchers to reproduce methods while safeguarding core datasets.
review: Partnership terms influence publication timelines and IP control; gaps include ensuring consistent enforcement across partners and preventing data access bottlenecks.

name: Analytics validation and cross-cohort benchmarking
consequences: Formal validation elevates methodological credibility and reproducibility, enabling robust phenotyping; however, it may slow iterations and require external data access commitments.
options: Establish a formal validation plan with predefined event-triage metrics and independent scoring audits to ensure reproducibility.
Implement a rolling six-month performance review with recalibration triggers when sensitivity or specificity drift is detected.
Pilot cross-site replication using matched external datasets to assess generalizability of parasomnia phenotyping across other populations.
review: Validation rigor strengthens credibility but adds latency; gaps include how to resolve discrepancies between internal scorers and external benchmarks when conflicts arise.

name: Conditional expansion of suites based on pilot data quality and safety metrics
consequences: Expanding capacity beyond eight suites will enable larger cohorts and more robust longitudinal data, but only if pilot data quality, annotation throughput, and safety metrics are consistently met. A failure to meet these thresholds risks underutilization of new suites and a spike in post-event review workload that strains staffing. The downstream effect could delay Aim 2 analyses and erode early data quality momentum.
options: Expand to 12 suites only after the pilot demonstrates consistent data quality across nights, acceptable false-alarm rates, and robust annotation throughput in two consecutive cohorts.
Conduct an independent data-quality audit before any capacity increase to ensure reproducibility and safeguard against calibration drift across sensors.
Maintain eight suites while aggressively improving scoring throughput and enrollment efficiency to buy time before expansion.
review: Gating expansion concentrates risk on pilot outcomes; the three options leave unaddressed the possibility that pilot cohorts do not generalize across a larger facility, especially if late-batch nights introduce new noise.

name: Adaptive event-triage enhancement through staged validation
consequences: A staged validation approach for event-triage will gradually improve accuracy and reduce manual load, but initial deployment may delay full automation gains and keep part of the review work manual longer. If calibration is not aligned with real-world data, false positives or missed events could erode trust in the tool and slow downstream analyses.
options: Pilot a machine-assisted scoring workflow that flags high-likelihood parasomnia events for rapid dual scoring by the team.
Implement iterative error-analysis sprints to methodically reduce false positives and improve true-positive capture before full deployment.
Adopt a tiered review schedule where borderline events receive expedited expert adjudication within 24 hours of detection.
review: The trade-off is between speed and accuracy: faster automation may come at the cost of initial misclassifications, and the three options leave gaps in how to handle persistent edge cases.

name: Privacy-first data governance with phased access and embargoes
consequences: A privacy-forward governance approach enables broader collaboration with controlled privacy, but increases governance overhead and can slow data release timelines, potentially delaying external replication. The governance burden may also divert resources from core data collection tasks if not properly scoped.
options: Establish a data-use agreement framework that permits broader research access only after de-identification and ethics approvals are secured.
Create a controlled-access repository with multiple access tiers and time-based embargoes on video data to protect privacy.
Pilot a regional data-sharing consortium with partner sites under joint governance to exchange only structured physiological data.
review: The primary trade-off is speed versus privacy; three options defer broader sharing, but do not fully resolve how to balance rapid dissemination with privacy guarantees.

name: Diverse recruitment channels to stabilize enrollment and representativeness
consequences: Diversifying recruitment channels reduces the risk of slow enrollment and improves cohort representativeness, but expands screening complexity and can introduce greater heterogeneity in data. The downstream effect is potential variability in event yield and comparability across subgroups.
options: Extend referrals to regional sleep clinics and primary care networks with standardized pre-screening to boost eligible participant flow.
Engage patient advocacy groups to raise awareness, decrease screening drop-off, and diversify participant demographics.
Implement matched-control enrollment incentives and streamlined consent workflows to improve recruitment efficiency.
review: The trade-off is breadth versus consistency; while wider channels may improve numbers, they may challenge uniform pre-screening and baseline comparability across cohorts.

name: Phased equipment procurement aligned with pilot milestones
consequences: Phased procurement controls capital expenditure and minimizes waste, but may constrain early data capture capabilities and delay enhanced nights. Delayed upgrades can slow method validation and comparison against full-capacity benchmarks.
options: Withhold major PSG equipment purchases until pilot nights prove reliable synchronization and low downtime across streams.
Stagger sensor-stack acquisitions with upgrades triggered by post-pilot lessons to minimize wasted spend.
Pursue modular sensor configurations that allow rapid component replacement without disrupting ongoing nights.
review: The main trade-off is cost containment versus speed to richer data; the options leave unaddressed the risk of future supply chain delays affecting critical milestones.

name: Staffing model optimization for safety and data throughput
consequences: Optimizing staffing improves safety and data throughput, but adds logistical complexity and higher administrative burden. If not well managed, costs may outpace budgeted allocations and scheduling conflicts could affect data capture quality.
options: Implement cross-trained night-shift teams to maintain full eight-suite coverage with flexible responder capacity.
Institute regular safety drills and third-party audits to verify compliance, improve response times, and reduce variability in staffing.
Create a pool of on-call technicians to cover peak data loads during enhanced nights while preserving core staffing stability.
review: The trade-off is flexibility and resilience versus administrative overhead; the options do not specify how to quantify staffing efficiency gains or budgetary impact.
